primary: Machine-learning researchers from other subfields (adjacent researchers): they know general ML, deep learning, standard evaluation practice and statistics, but not information retrieval's subfield-specific terminology, datasets, or prior work.
secondary: No specific venue/reviewer pool was given for this run; treated as careful adjacent-field readers who would check that numbers and comparisons are stated precisely and traceable (see plan/venue_profile.yaml, generic profile).
tertiary: Future readers who want a self-contained account of what BEIR is, what it found, and its main limits, without needing to read the original IR-venue paper.
assumed_known: supervised fine-tuning of pretrained Transformer encoders (e.g. BERT)
train/dev/test evaluation protocol and the general idea of a benchmark suite
zero-shot evaluation as a general ML concept
standard ML evaluation practice and statistics (e.g. what an average over a heterogeneous set of tasks summarizes, why single-run comparisons are less conclusive than replicated ones)
basic ranking/contrastive-loss intuition from representation learning
not_assumed: information-retrieval-specific terminology (qrels, pooling, bi-encoder vs. cross-encoder, late interaction, lexical gap, Hole@k)
IR evaluation metrics (nDCG@k, MRR, MAP) and why they differ from classification metrics
the specific datasets and architectures compared (BM25, DPR, ANCE, TAS-B, ColBERT, etc.)
prior IR benchmarks (MultiReQA, KILT) and how BEIR differs from them
source: given directly in the task instructions (AUDIENCE field); mapped to reader mode B per rce/skill/audience_model.md §2
notes: Because this is Mode B (not C/D), technical precision and full rigor are kept; only subfield-specific vocabulary, datasets and prior work need explicit definition/introduction. Statistics and general ML method concepts are not re-explained.
